articles.title: Arnold Schwarzenegger says Donald Trump asked him to campaign in 2016, recalls telling him ‘I cannot do that’ over climate change and pollution; says ‘I'm a Republican’
articles.summary: Actor and former California Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger has revealed why he refused to campaign for Donald Trump during his 2016 presidential run,
articles.body: Actor and former California Governor Arnold Schwarzenegger has revealed why he refused to campaign for Donald Trump during his 2016 presidential run, despite sharing a close friendship with him at the time. Appearing on Jimmy Kimmel Live! on Wednesday, November 11, Schwarzenegger said Trump's views on climate change and pollution went against everything he had worked towards for years. The 79-year-old actor also spoke about why he continues to identify as a traditional Republican despite disagreeing with the party's present-day direction, urging Democrats and Republicans to work together rather than prioritising party politics.Schwarzenegger, who became California's governor in November 2003, recalled that Trump had personally approached him during his 2016 presidential campaign, asking him to endorse his candidacy and campaign alongside him. The two had shared a good relationship, but Schwarzenegger said he could not support Trump because of their differences over environmental issues."We had a good relationship; we were very good friends. He asked me if I would go and endorse him and campaign with him," Schwarzenegger told Jimmy Kimmel.Recalling his response, he said he told Trump that although he wanted to remain friends, he disagreed with several things the businessman-turned-politician stood for.Schwarzenegger specifically pointed to Trump's position on climate change and pollution, explaining that environmental protection had been an important part of his own work for years."I said, 'You don't believe there is climate change. You don't believe the threat of pollution,'" he recalled, adding that pollution kills millions of people and cannot simply be ignored.He further said that he could not campaign for Trump because of that issue alone.Why Schwarzenegger still considers himself a traditional RepublicanDuring the conversation, Kimmel also asked Schwarzenegger whether he still considered himself a Republican despite his disagreements with the party's current political direction."Yeah, I'm a Republican, absolutely," he replied.Explaining what being a traditional Republican means to him, Schwarzenegger referred to the party's historical role in ending slavery and granting African Americans citizenship and voting rights.When Kimmel pointed out that these values appeared to be at odds with what the modern Republican Party represents, Schwarzenegger responded that he did not need to change his own philosophy.He also cited former US presidents Ronald Reagan and Richard Nixon, crediting Reagan with establishing California's Air Resources Board and Nixon with creating the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA)."Those are the kind of Republicans that used to go and work together with the Democrats and got things done. This is the kind of Republican that I am," he explained.Schwarzenegger urges Democrats and Republicans to work togetherThe actor also spoke about the growing political divide in the United States and said neither party had done enough to address major issues despite repeatedly gaining power.Referring to the Democrats' recent midterm gains, Schwarzenegger described the political shift as a "tidal wave or a tsunami" rather than simply a blue wave. He argued that political power keeps moving between Democrats and Republicans, but important problems remain unresolved.He specifically mentioned immigration reform, national debt and healthcare, saying successive administrations and lawmakers had failed to find lasting solutions.Schwarzenegger also expressed support for immigration reform and a healthcare system that ensures everyone has coverage. During the conversation, he disagreed with Kimmel over the Affordable Care Act, describing it as a well-intentioned attempt that had not adequately addressed rising healthcare costs.He maintained that neither party could achieve meaningful progress by acting alone."What you have to do is the Democrats and the Republicans have to work together like we did when I was governor of California," he said.He further emphasised that elected representatives should focus on serving citizens rather than their political parties."You have to get together and accomplish and be a public servant rather than a party servant. There's a difference," he added.Schwarzenegger had endorsed Kamala Harris in 2024Despite identifying as a Republican, Schwarzenegger has previously taken positions that put him at odds with the party's presidential leadership. During the 2024 US presidential election, he publicly endorsed Democratic candidate Kamala Harris and her running mate Tim Walz.His latest remarks reinforce his position that political beliefs should not necessarily be dictated by party loyalty. The actor has repeatedly spoken about the importance of environmental protection and bipartisan cooperation.Schwarzenegger appeared on Jimmy Kimmel Live! to promote his upcoming film The Man With the Bag. His conversation with Kimmel covered his Hollywood career, political identity, friendship with Trump and his views on the changing Republican Party.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Billionaire sheikh’s wife loses £8.3 million London mansion battle after claiming her husband gifted her the property under Islamic custom, leaving the home exposed to his £80 million business debt
articles.summary: Makiyah Al Jaber has lost a High Court battle over an £8.3 million London mansion after arguing that her billionaire husband had gifted her the property
articles.body: Makiyah Al Jaber has lost a High Court battle over an £8.3 million London mansion after arguing that her billionaire husband had gifted her the property under Islamic custom. The dispute centred on whether the family home, despite being registered in Sheikh Mohamed Bin Issa Al Jaber’s name, was actually owned by his wife and therefore protected from claims against his business debts. The ruling has left her facing the possibility of losing the residence where she has lived for more than three decades and raised their three children.Why the billionaire sheikh’s wife lost the London mansion ownership battleThe case concerned a property on Winnington Road in Hampstead Garden Suburb, north London. According to The Independent, the house is valued at £8.3 million. It sits on a street that overtook the nearby Bishop’s Avenue, widely known as Billionaires’ Row, as Britain’s most expensive residential street in 2025.Makiyah Al Jaber maintained that the mansion belonged to her in practice, even though the legal title was held solely by her husband. She said the house had been purchased specifically for her in accordance with an Islamic custom under which a husband is responsible for providing a home for his wife, with the property understood to belong to her.Her argument became particularly important after financial claims against her husband threatened the family residence.The business debts behind the property disputeThe Independent reported that Sheikh Mohamed Bin Issa Al Jaber’s company, MBI International & Partners Inc, an offshore business based in the British Virgin Islands, went into liquidation in 2017 after having ceased trading.A High Court judgment in 2023 established that the company’s liquidators were owed money by the sheikh in connection with valuable shares transferred out of the business in 2016, before its liquidation. The debt subsequently grew to approximately £80 million.The liquidators sought to secure repayment against the London mansion. An interim charging order was placed on the property in 2023, although further related legal proceedings delayed a final decision for almost three years.The couple disputed the attempt to use the house to settle the debts, arguing that its ownership should not be treated as belonging to the sheikh simply because it was registered in his name.What Makiyah Al Jaber told the court about the houseDuring the hearing, Makiyah Al Jaber explained that her husband had asked her to choose a house and promised to purchase it for her. She said she had always understood that the property was hers and that he could not sell it, even if their marriage ended.According to The Independent, she presented three separate arguments in support of her claim. The first was that the house had been provided to her under Islamic custom. The second concerned her contribution to the property over the years, including managing renovations and maintaining the home for the family.She also argued that she had relied on the understanding that the house belonged to her, leaving her at a disadvantage after moving to London from Saudi Arabia in 1992 and building her family life there.The judge rejected the Islamic custom argumentDeputy Master Joanna Valentine rejected the claim that the house was beneficially owned by Makiyah Al Jaber. The judge explained that legal ownership normally determines beneficial ownership unless evidence establishes a different arrangement between the parties.The court was not satisfied that the claimed Islamic custom had been established through sufficient evidence. The judge said she had not received expert evidence explaining the existence or extent of such a custom and could not simply accept the wife's account as proof.She also stressed that even if such a tradition existed, the important question was what the husband and wife had actually understood and agreed about ownership of this particular property.The judge found that the sheikh had treated the mansion as his own asset in previous legal proceedings. That history weakened the argument that he had intended the house to belong to his wife in a legal sense.Renovations and years of family life did not establish ownershipMakiyah Al Jaber also argued that her long involvement with the property should give her a share in its ownership. She said she had overseen repeated renovations and improvements, adapting the house to accommodate the family's changing needs.The court accepted that she had managed maintenance and repairs and had devoted considerable time and effort to the home. However, those contributions did not establish an agreement between the couple that she would own the property.Her final argument was that she had suffered a disadvantage by relying on the belief that the house was hers. She said she had given up the opportunity to acquire another property and had invested years in maintaining and improving the mansion.The judge was not persuaded that this amounted to the necessary disadvantage under the legal principle she relied upon. She noted that the family's financial resources had been provided by the husband and found insufficient evidence that the wife had suffered a loss.The London mansion could still face a saleThe ruling established that the property belonged to Sheikh Mohamed Bin Issa Al Jaber both legally and beneficially, according to The Independent. The judge subsequently made a final charging order against the mansion, allowing it to serve as security for the business debt.However, the decision did not immediately mean that the property would be sold. The judge explained that a separate order would be required before a sale could take place to satisfy part of the outstanding debt. She also indicated that Makiyah Al Jaber's long occupation of the house could be considered if a sale were pursued.The ruling leaves the family residence exposed to the financial claims against the sheikh.The couple ordered to share the legal costsThe court also addressed the substantial expenses arising from the ownership dispute. The liquidators' legal costs were reported to be approximately £744,000, a figure that the sheikh's legal representatives described as exceptionally high.Both husband and wife argued that the other should be responsible for paying the costs. Makiyah Al Jaber maintained that her husband should bear the expense because he was her spouse, while the sheikh argued that he had merely supported her position.The judge ordered them to be jointly responsible for the costs and directed that 40% of the liquidators' bill, amounting to just under £300,000, be paid upfront.You use AI every day. articles.title: A Montana father sought to change his parenting plan after his former wife moved, arguing it made visits harder; the state Supreme Court ruled that 10 extra driving miles were not enough to reopen the arrangement
articles.summary: Adding just 10 miles to a driving route is not a major enough change to justify modifying an existing parenting plan, the Montana Supreme Court has ruled.
articles.body: Adding just 10 miles to a driving route is not a major enough change to justify modifying an existing parenting plan, the Montana Supreme Court has ruled. The decision followed an appeal in case DA 26-0231 (In re the Marriage of Aikins), which began in the Ninth Judicial District Court in Toole County. Justin L. Aikins asked the court to change his existing parenting schedule after his former wife, Loralee J. Aikins (now Loralee J. Lords), moved to a different home. He argued that the extra distance made it harder for him to spend time with their children. District Judge Gregory L. Bonilla initially rejected the father's request to change the parenting plan. Aikins then appealed to Montana's highest court. Chief Justice Cory Swanson assigned the case to a panel of five justices to decide whether the lower court had made a mistake by refusing to review the parenting schedule. After reviewing the case, the Montana Supreme Court upheld the lower court's decision. The justices ruled that adding 10 miles to a journey was not enough to meet the legal requirements for changing a final parenting plan.Legal threshold for modifying parenting plansUnder Montana family law, courts must focus on keeping children's lives stable. An existing parenting agreement cannot be changed unless there is a major change in circumstances that affects the child's well-being or the parents' ability to care for them. In his appeal, Justin Aikins argued that his former wife's move had created practical problems with picking up and dropping off the children. He said the extra travel had changed the arrangements that were in place when the original agreement was made. He asked the court to review the schedule and change the travel arrangements or adjust parenting time to account for the additional driving. However, the Supreme Court found that small changes in location within the same local area were not enough to reopen a court order. The justices explained that slightly longer journeys are a normal part of everyday life. Such changes do not automatically harm a child or make an existing parenting schedule impossible to follow.Proceedings in the Ninth Judicial DistrictThe dispute began as part of ongoing legal proceedings following the divorce in Toole County, under District Court Cause No. DR-2018-019. After the original divorce and custody orders were made, both parents followed an agreed schedule for several years before the mother moved. When Loralee Lords changed her home address, Justin Aikins filed a request with the Ninth Judicial District Court to change the parenting arrangements. During hearings before Judge Bonilla, the court looked at exactly how much extra travel the move had created. The findings showed that the distance between the two homes had increased by about 10 miles. Judge Bonilla decided that the small increase in driving distance did not amount to a major change affecting the child's best interests. After the District Court rejected his request, Aikins filed an appeal with the Montana Supreme Court in April 2026. He represented himself without a lawyer. Loralee Lords, meanwhile, had legal representation from the Great Falls law firm Faure Holden Attorneys at Law, PC.Court mediation and final panel reviewBefore deciding the appeal, the case went through a required mediation process under the Montana Rules of Appellate Procedure. Supreme Court records show that an initial mediator appointment was cancelled in May 2026. The two parties then agreed to work with mediator Tamara Barkus. However, the mediation did not lead to an agreement between the parents. The mediator filed a report confirming that the dispute remained unresolved. The case then returned to the usual appeals process.Both sides submitted their written arguments during the summer of 2026. Chief Justice Cory Swanson later issued an order sending the case to a panel of five justices for a decision based on those written arguments. The court reviewed whether the lower court had correctly followed Montana's existing legal rules on relocation and parental rights. By upholding Judge Bonilla's decision, the panel reinforced the rules that apply to custody disputes across Montana. The justices confirmed that small changes in travel distance cannot automatically be used by parents with joint or shared custody arrangements as a reason to reopen an established parenting schedule. The ruling sets a clear limit for future family law disputes across the state. It shows that small moves of just a few miles are not enough to reopen settled custody cases unless there is other evidence showing a direct negative effect on the child's well-being.You use AI every day.
